title: Ukiah Club In Mendocino County To Stay Open With Support Of County Supervisors -- Still Faces Federal Action

content_html_sanitized:
By MIKE GENIELLA

Ukiah Press Democrat staff writer

A cannabis club in Ukiah, following the lead of a San Francisco club that has been in the middle of high-profile court fight, will remain open in the face of continuing legal pressure to close down.

A San Francisco judge on Thursday ordered closure of the city’s Cannabis Cultivators Club in the wake of a new state Supreme Court decision decreeing such operations illegal. But the owner, who wrote the medical marijuana initiative, vowed to stay open.

The court edict will affect all cannibis clubs, including the Ukiah Cannabis Buyers Club, state Attorney General Dan Lungren said Thursday.

But Mendocino County sheriff’s representatives said they need further clarification before attempting to shut down an operation that recently received the tacit endorsement of the county Board of Supervisors as long as it complies with terms of Proposition 215, which allowed the medical use of marijuana.

Since passage of the statewide measure in 1996, the Ukiah club has become the North Coast’s largest marijuana provider for people with medical prescriptions.

""Because of the nature of the issues surrounding Proposition 215, we decided soon after it was passed that our approach would be one of restraint. We will continue that until we have clear direction from the Attorney General’s Office," said sheriff’s Capt. Kevin Broin.

Ukiah Cannabis Club representatives said Thursday that unless advised otherwise by their attorneys, they plan to continue dispensing pot to people with medical prescriptions.

""We are continuing with our operation. We are not closing down," said Marvin Lehrman, director of the Ukiah Cannibis Buyers Club. The club has about 300 registered members, but not all of them are regular patrons, said Lehrman.

In a blow to cannibis club supporters, state Supreme Court justices declared Wednesday that Proposition 215 does not allow anyone to sell marijuana and does not allow a commercial enterprise, even if nonprofit, to furnish pot by acting as a ""primary caregiver" as allowed under the proposition.

In wake of Wednesday’s decision, the AG’s office asked a state court to issue a preliminary injunction against San Francisco’s cannibis club, and its founder, Dennis Peron.

But whether the Attorney General will take specific action against five other cannibis clubs in Northern California, including Ukiah, remained unclear.

Spokesman Matt Ross said, ""We’ve always said that local authorities can make their own decisions once we won in court."

The Supreme Court decision is the latest setback for cannibis club supporters.

In January, Ukiah’s cannibis club was among six cited by federal authorities who filed civil lawsuits in federal court seeking closure of the clubs because their distribution of marijuana violated federal drug laws. A further hearing on a federal request for an injunction against club operations is scheduled March 20.

""Clearly, the state Supreme Court decision was not helpful to the clubs," said Mendocino County attorney David Nelson, who represents the Ukiah club.

But Nelson said he found it interesting that Supreme Court justices in their ruling did not question the validity of Proposition 215.

""So what we have is a situation where marijuana for medical purposes is allowed under state law, but how to get it to people who need it remains unclear," said Nelson.
